summary: Today’s pulse tracks ‘Not afraid of controversy’: Edinburgh fringe rejects calls to cancel Amanda Knox comedy, Trump administration to pay German firm $1.2bn to halt US wind projects, and ByteDance trains massive AI model in bid to rival Anthropic. Across Guardian, BBC, and Ars Technica, the strongest repeated signals are blanche, trump, and cassidy. In the background, The world's biggest solar telescope caught vortexes on the Sun's surface and Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign defence pact keep the wider picture in motion.

headlines.title: ‘Not afraid of controversy’: Edinburgh fringe rejects calls to cancel Amanda Knox comedy
headlines.description: Festival organisers defend show after criticism from sister of Meredith Kercher, Knox’s murdered former flatmate The Edinburgh festival fringe said it was “not afraid of controversy” after calls to cancel a sold-out show by Amanda Knox , who was falsely imprisoned for the 2007 murder of her flatmate Meredith Kercher in Italy. Knox’s comedy show, Cartwheel, has been condemned by Kercher’s family, with her sister, Stephanie, saying it “normalises and trivialises violence against women”. A petition calling for it to be cancelled has been signed by more than 6,000 people.

headlines.title: Trump administration to pay German firm $1.2bn to halt US wind projects
headlines.description: The RWE payout is the latest in a string of deals cancelling wind energy projects, a power source long derided by Trump.

headlines.title: Blanche’s attorney general confirmation in jeopardy after Republican senators back away from Trump’s nominee – live
headlines.description: Todd Blanche can’t afford another Republican deflection after Lisa Murkowski ⁠and Susan Collins voice opposition; all eyes on Bill Cassidy, who could sink nomination Murkowski won’t support Blanche’s attorney general bid So far the only other holdout is Senator Bill Cassidy – a GOP lawmaker from Louisiana. Cassidy, a former physician, said this week he’s concerned about Blanche’s ability to lead the justice department independently, considering he once served as Donald Trump’s personal lawyer.

headlinePool.title: Employers unexpectedly cut 23,000 jobs in a sign of a wilting labor market
headlinePool.description: U.S. employers cut 23,000 jobs in July, and job gains for the two previous months were weaker than initially reported, according to a report Friday from the Labor Department.

headlinePool.title: US airfares expected to stay high even if Iran ceasefire drops oil prices, experts say
headlinePool.description: Domestic flights cost 26.5% more than last year, data shows, amid demand for travel and reduced oil refining capacity Even if a lasting ceasefire between the US and Iran lowers oil prices , travelers hoping to snag cheaper airfare should buckle their seatbelts and expect continued turbulence . US domestic airfares are 26.5% higher than a year ago, according to June’s consumer price index data, and analysts say prices globally are up 25-30% compared with 2025.

headlinePool.title: ‘It didn’t need to end this way’: mother of US teen trafficked and killed decries police failures
headlinePool.description: Robyn Cory says daughter Kristen was not protected, amid questions about why it took six years to identify remains The family of Kristen Galvan, a 15-year-old Houston girl who was sex trafficked and murdered, says law enforcement failed her twice by not protecting her after she gave forensic interviews about her traffickers, and later by taking more than six years to identify her remains. The Texas attorney general’s office announced on 28 July that Kristen’s remains had been positively identified using advanced DNA testing conducted over the past year. Parts of her skull, clothing and an earring were found beneath a bridge beside a jogging trail in Missouri City, about 10 miles outside Houston.

headlinePool.title: The White House’s plan to vet potentially dangerous AI is cloaked in secrecy
headlinePool.description: A Trump administration framework on AI testing leaves a lack of transparency – and plenty of open questions After months of talking with tech industry leaders, the Trump administration finalized a framework this week for how it will test new artificial intelligence models for safety and cybersecurity risks. So far, the White House is keeping details of the framework private, in a blow to transparency and potential boon for secretive AI companies. On Tuesday, staff from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, Nvidia and Microsoft attended a private meeting with White House officials to review the AI framework. Multiple outlets have since reported that although the volunteer vetting process for new AI models has been settled, the White House does not plan to release its policy publicly and will only share testing criteria with a select few tech companies.

headlinePool.title: Trump is losing his war on wind power
headlinePool.description: A court rules that a hold on all wind projects clearly violates the law.

headlinePool.title: Labour minister denies Burnham ‘too blokey’ – UK politics live
headlinePool.description: Home Office minister Anna Turley says PM is ‘authentic’ and praises video of him discussing bar snacks with John Healey Scottish Labour has “turned to rubble”, one of the party’s leadership contenders has claimed. Monica Lennon still does not have enough support to secure a spot on the ballot to take on MSPs Michael Marra and Joe Fagan in the contest to succeed Anas Sarwar.

headlinePool.title: Scramble to house hundreds camping in Rome heatwave after squat eviction
headlinePool.description: Officials try to find homes for residents as talks to save social assistance hub collapse amid government crackdown Rome authorities are scrambling to find homes for hundreds of people sleeping in tents in extreme heat after talks aimed at saving Italy’s most high-profile centre for housing and social assistance collapsed amid a crackdown by Giorgia Meloni’s government on squatted buildings. The approximately 400 evicted residents of Spin Time Labs, located in a 10-floor building in Rome’s Esquilino district occupied by grassroots groups since 2013, will not be allowed to move back in after its private owner refused Rome council’s offer to buy the property. The residents were forced out at the end of last month.

headlinePool.title: First Thing: Soaring oil profits from US-Iran conflict drive calls for windfall tax
headlinePool.description: Environmentalists and activists furious as Trump’s policies raise costs for Americans. Plus, the masterpiece that was left lying in museum storage Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here Good morning. Donald Trump’s statement that oil companies have made “too much money” from the Iran war has angered environmentalists , who say his policies were designed to benefit those very corporations. Americans have paid more than $78bn more at the pump since the start of the Iran war, according to a Brown University tracker. A recent analysis from the environmental advocacy group Climate Power and the Center for American Progress Action Fund, a liberal thinktank, found that Trump’s policies had cost the average American family $285 more when filling up their cars. What policies has Trump enacted to help the oil industry? Since re-entering the White House last year, he has eased dozens of restrictions and regulations on fossil fuel expansion, exempted fossil fuel producers from environmental rules, and signed an executive order last year directing the attorney general to prioritize blocking climate lawsuits targeting oil majors. Trump has also personally invested in major oil companies. What did the supreme court previously rule? In the court’s June decision, the chief justice, John Roberts, said Trump’s first order violated the 14th amendment of the US constitution. “Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights – to freely participate in our political community,” he wrote. “The framers of the 14th amendment extended that promise to ‘every free-born person in this land’. We keep that promise today.”

headlinePool.title: William Orbit, pop producer for Madonna, All Saints and more, dies aged 69
headlinePool.description: Musician’s projects included Madonna’s Ray of Light, Blur’s 13 and All Saints’ chart-topping singles Pure Shores and Black Coffee William Orbit, the British music producer whose dreamy yet propulsive style invigorated work by Madonna, Blur, All Saints, U2 and more, has died aged 69. A statement on his social media, attributed to family and friends, said he died at home on 23 July. “He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness,” the statement read. No cause of death was given.
